Dwight Eisenhower. From 1890 to 1969, Eisenhower was an American military commander and statesman who led the Supreme Allied Command in Europe during World War II and served as the 34th President of the United States from 1953 to 1961. His presidency emphasized stability during the Cold War, infrastructure development, and a doctrine of "massive retaliation" against Soviet expansion.

During World War II, Eisenhower served as Supreme Commander of the Allied Forces in Europe, orchestrating the D-Day invasion and the final campaign against Nazi Germany. In his farewell address as President, he popularized the phrase "military-industrial complex," warning against the concentration of power in defense industries and the military.

His presidency launched the Interstate Highway System, one of the largest public works projects in history, nominally justified by Cold War defense needs. He endorsed the domino theory and the doctrine of "massive retaliation," which relied on nuclear weapons to deter Soviet aggression and communist expansion. At the same time, he maintained a policy of "peaceful coexistence" with the Soviet Union, even while authorizing covert CIA operations in Iran and Guatemala to counter Soviet-backed movements.

Eisenhower proposed the "Open Skies" initiative to the Soviets in 1955, offering mutual air reconnaissance to reduce Cold War tensions, though the USSR rejected it. However, he faced the U-2 spy plane incident in 1960, when a Soviet surface-to-air missile shot down an American reconnaissance aircraft, damaging Cold War thaw efforts. His Vice President, Richard Nixon, would later succeed him with a more aggressively anti-communist foreign policy.
